# Memory Ordering: Why Code Runs Out of Order and What to Do About It

Last verified: 2026-10-30 against cppreference std::memory_order, cppreference std::mutex::unlock and C while-loop pages, kernel.org memory-barriers.txt, Rust std::sync::atomic docs, Preshing's x86 reordering article, Linux tools/memory-model explanation.txt and the loom README. Every program and assembly listing was re-run or re-compiled on macOS, Apple M4, clang.

Starts from: lessons 00 to 02 (a race, a lock, an atomic). Nothing else.

## The problem and why it matters

Lesson 02 said an atomic covers one value and does not order the memory around it. That sentence hides the strangest thing in this module: **two threads can disagree about the order in which things happened**, even when each thread's code is correct line by line. If you publish data and then set a "ready" flag, another thread can see the flag set and still read old data. You will meet this in reviews of lock-free code, in channel and lock internals, and in "works on my laptop" bugs that only show on other hardware.

## First principles

1. **The compiler is allowed to rearrange your code.** Its only promise is that a *single thread* cannot tell the difference. It may delete reads it thinks are redundant, move writes, or merge them (Evidence 1 shows one deleting a whole loop). The kernel docs give an example: "The compiler is within its rights to reorder loads and stores to the same variable, and in some cases".
2. **The CPU is allowed to rearrange memory accesses too.** The kernel docs: CPUs "can use a variety of tricks to improve performance, including reordering". What is sourced is the effect: Preshing's summary of Intel's x86 rules says each processor "is allowed to delay the effect of a store past any load from a different location", and the Linux memory-model docs say the store-buffering outcome in Evidence 2 "does sometimes occur on x86 and SPARC systems". This lesson does not explain the hardware mechanism behind it. Each core keeps its own view consistent (kernel docs: "Overlapping loads and stores within a particular CPU will appear to be ordered within that CPU"), but a *different* core can see the effects in another order.
3. **Why allow it?** Speed (the kernel docs: CPUs use these tricks "to improve performance"). Rearranging is invisible to one thread, so hardware and compilers do it freely.
4. **A memory model is the contract.** It says which rearrangements the programmer must be protected from, and how to ask for protection: by marking operations with an *ordering* (relaxed, release, acquire, sequentially consistent). Rust follows the C++20 rules for this, without "consume" (its docs: "Rust atomics currently follow the same rules as C++20 atomics").
5. **Ordering is about visibility, not about waiting.** It does not make threads wait for each other. It constrains what one thread may observe about another's writes.

## How it works

### Evidence 1: the compiler deletes your wait loop

```c
int ready;                                         /* plain int */
void wait_plain(void) { while (!ready) { } }       /* spin until another thread sets it */
```

Compiled with `clang -O2 -S` on this Mac, the whole function body is:

```text
_wait_plain:
	ret
```

Captured here. The compiler reasoned "nothing in this thread changes `ready`, so the loop either exits at once or never". Per cppreference, a program with an endless loop that has no observable behavior (I/O, volatile accesses, atomic or synchronization operations) has undefined behavior, "This allows the compilers to optimize out all unobservable loops without proving that they terminate" (the exception is a constant condition like `while(true)`). So the compiler may assume the loop ends, and it removed the waiting. With `atomic_int` and a relaxed load, the loop survives (`ldr w9, [x8]` then `cbz w9, <back to the load>`). Lesson: a plain variable is not a way to signal between threads; an atomic is. (This is also why the data race in lesson 00 is "undefined behavior".)

### Evidence 2: two threads disagree about the order

Classic test (called store buffering, after the effect it exposes). Start with x = 0, y = 0:

```
  thread A            thread B
  x = 1               y = 1
  r1 = y              r2 = x
```

If all steps ran in some single interleaving, whoever goes second must see the other's write, so `r1 == 0 && r2 == 0` is impossible. Run it 200,000 times (compile: `clang -O2 -pthread sb.c`, add `-DSEQ` for the strict version):

```c
#include <pthread.h>
#include <stdatomic.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#ifdef SEQ
#define ORD memory_order_seq_cst
#else
#define ORD memory_order_relaxed
#endif
#define ROUNDS 200000
atomic_int x, y, go, done;
int r1, r2;
void *thread_a(void *p) {
    for (int i = 1; i <= ROUNDS; i++) {
        while (atomic_load(&go) != i) ;           // wait for start signal
        atomic_store_explicit(&x, 1, ORD);        // x = 1
        r1 = atomic_load_explicit(&y, ORD);       // r1 = y
        atomic_fetch_add(&done, 1);
    }
    return p;
}
void *thread_b(void *p) {
    for (int i = 1; i <= ROUNDS; i++) {
        while (atomic_load(&go) != i) ;
        atomic_store_explicit(&y, 1, ORD);        // y = 1
        r2 = atomic_load_explicit(&x, ORD);       // r2 = x
        atomic_fetch_add(&done, 1);
    }
    return p;
}
int main(void) {
    pthread_t a, b;
    pthread_create(&a, 0, thread_a, 0);
    pthread_create(&b, 0, thread_b, 0);
    long both_zero = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i <= ROUNDS; i++) {
        atomic_store(&x, 0); atomic_store(&y, 0); atomic_store(&done, 0);
        atomic_store(&go, i);                     // release both threads at once
        while (atomic_load(&done) != 2) ;
        if (r1 == 0 && r2 == 0) both_zero++;
    }
    printf("r1==0 && r2==0 in %ld of %d rounds\n", both_zero, ROUNDS);
}
```

```text
relaxed:  r1==0 && r2==0 in 199752 of 200000 rounds
relaxed:  r1==0 && r2==0 in 199973 of 200000 rounds
relaxed:  r1==0 && r2==0 in 199969 of 200000 rounds
seq_cst:  r1==0 && r2==0 in 0 of 200000 rounds   (3 of 3 runs)
```

Re-run 2026-10-29 on macOS, Apple M4. The "impossible" outcome happened almost every round under relaxed. My guess (not tested) is that the harness releases both threads at the same instant, so each read runs before the other thread's write has become visible. Real code does not hit it that often. With `seq_cst` it never happened. Your counts will differ; x86 was not run here, but the Linux kernel's memory-model docs say this outcome "does sometimes occur on x86 and SPARC systems" (under the TSO model).

### The ordering levels

```
 weakest                                          strongest
 relaxed ──▶ release/acquire ──▶ seq_cst
 "atomic,    "publish, then      "one global order
  nothing     consume"            everyone agrees on"
  else"
```

From cppreference:
- **Relaxed**: "no synchronization or ordering constraints imposed on other reads or writes, only this operation's atomicity is guaranteed".
- **Release** (on a store): "no reads or writes in the current thread can be reordered after this store"; "All writes in the current thread are visible in other threads that acquire the same atomic variable".
- **Acquire** (on a load): "no reads or writes in the current thread can be reordered before this load".
- **Sequentially consistent**: acquire and release plus "a single total order exists in which all threads observe all modifications in the same order". It is the default for C++ atomics and costs more on some hardware ("Total sequential ordering requires a full memory fence CPU instruction on all multi-core systems"): measure before weakening it.

### Release and acquire as a hand-off

```
 writer thread                reader thread
 data = 42
 flag.store(1, release) ──┐
                          └─▶ flag.load(acquire) == 1
                              read data  -> 42, guaranteed
```

cppreference: "once the atomic load is completed, thread B is guaranteed to see everything thread A wrote to memory", but only "if B actually returns the value that A stored, or a value from later in the release sequence". Both sides are needed. A mutex is this same pattern: unlock "synchronizes-with" any subsequent lock of the same mutex (cppreference `std::mutex::unlock`; lesson 01).

What the compiler actually emitted on this ARM Mac for the stores and loads (`clang -O2 -S`):

```text
relaxed store of flag:  str   w9, [x8]
release store of flag:  stlr  w9, [x8]
relaxed load of flag:   ldr   w0, [x8]
acquire load of flag:   ldapr w0, [x8]
```

Captured here. The release and acquire versions use special instructions that carry the ordering. I also tried the data-then-flag test directly (2,000,000 rounds, relaxed, my own harness, 3 runs): the reader saw the flag set between about 30,000 and 1,000,000 times per run and **never** saw stale data. So I could **not** reproduce that failure on this machine, and that is the lesson: a test that passes shows nothing about code that is wrong by the model. That is why `rust-systems/04-lock-free-structures` uses `loom`, which "runs a test many times, permuting the possible concurrent executions of that test under the C11 memory model". Its README says "Loom currently does not implement the full C11 memory model", and that "there can be a bug in the checked code even if Loom says there is no bug", so a clean loom run is evidence, not proof.

### Picking an ordering

| Situation | Ordering |
|---|---|
| Counter nobody branches on | relaxed |
| "Data is ready" flag or pointer | release store, acquire load |
| Unsure, several flags, a global order needed | seq_cst (default) |
| Lock-protected data | the lock does it |

Same as `rust-systems/04`: default to the strongest, weaken with evidence.

## Worked failure scenario

**Symptom:** a service sets `config_version` (relaxed) after writing a new config; readers load the version, see the change, and read the config. About one in millions of requests sees half-initialized config, never in tests.

1. **Smell:** an atomic acting as a "data ready" flag, using relaxed.
2. **Why it hides:** my own data-and-flag test found no stale read on this ARM Mac. The model allows the failure even when one machine never shows it.
3. **Prove it:** model the pair in `loom` (see `rust-systems/04`).
4. **Fix:** store the version with release after writing, load with acquire; or swap the whole config behind one `Arc` so nothing needs ordering.
5. **Prevent:** one small tested type owns the publication.

## Tradeoffs

| Use when | Avoid when |
|---|---|
| relaxed: statistics counters | Anything another thread uses to decide that other data is ready |
| release/acquire: publish and consume | You cannot explain the hand-off in one sentence: use seq_cst |
| seq_cst: default, hard cases | A measured hot path where weaker is proven safe |
| A mutex or channel: skip ordering | Hot-path lock cost is measured and unacceptable |

## Interview questions

1. Why can a CPU or compiler reorder operations at all? *Outline:* single-thread illusion; speed; compilers delete or move; CPUs may let a store take effect after a later load.
2. What does release/acquire guarantee? *Outline:* writes before the release visible after the matching acquire reads that value.
3. Show me a failure with relaxed. *Outline:* publish data + flag; or store-buffering test.
4. Why does my test pass but the code is wrong? *Outline:* the model permits it, hardware or timing may not show it; use `loom`, sanitizers.
5. relaxed vs seq_cst for a stats counter? *Outline:* relaxed; nobody orders other data on it.

**Whiteboard exercise:** two threads, `data` then `flag`. Draw the arrow Release/Acquire creates, then erase it (relaxed) and draw how the reader sees flag set but data stale.

## Checklist

1. I can say why compilers and CPUs reorder, in two sentences.
2. I can explain relaxed, release, acquire and seq_cst without jargon.
3. I can draw the data-and-flag hand-off.
4. I can explain why a passing test is weak evidence here.
5. I know to default to seq_cst and to prefer a lock or channel.

## Common wrong answers

- "Atomic means ordered." Atomic means indivisible; ordering is separate.
- "The CPU runs my lines in order." Only as seen by that one thread.
- "It works on my machine, so the ordering is right." The model decides, not one machine.
- "A plain flag variable is enough to signal another thread." The compiler may delete the wait loop (evidence 1).
